setupSteps: Find the station: a captain's chair has a back pad, two forearm pads with handles at the front, and sometimes a step. Check the pads are not torn and the frame is not wobbling (check both arm pads are stable, per coaching sources).
Step up: stand on the floor or step, back to the pad, and place your forearms on the two pads, elbows under your shoulders (est.). Hold the handles loosely.
Back: press your whole back, from lower back to shoulder blades, against the back pad. Head rests lightly on the pad or stays in line with the spine.
Shoulders: keep them down and away from your ears; do not hunch.
Legs: lift your feet off the floor, so your legs hang, knees soft. Beginner version: keep your knees bent about 90 degrees (est.) and your feet together.
Brace: gently tighten the belly as if preparing to cough.
Weight: none for beginners; no ankle weights.
Spotter: not needed for the bent-knee version; stay near the floor so you can step down.
Step-down plan: know how you will get down: lower your feet to the floor or step, then take your arms off the pads.

steps.title: Get on the chair
steps.action: Stand with your back to the pad and place your forearms on the arm pads.
steps.feel: Weight on the forearms, back against the pad.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat on the pad, elbows under the shoulders. Front: forearms level, shoulders even.

steps.title: Set the shoulders
steps.action: Pull the shoulders down, away from the ears, and hold the handles lightly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ears over shoulders. Front: shoulders level and low.

steps.title: Lift the feet
steps.action: Bend the knees to about 90 degrees and lift your feet off the floor so you hang from the forearm pads.
steps.feel: Weight on the pads and back pad, legs light.
steps.visualCheck: Side: thighs pointing down, knees bent, back still on the pad.

steps.title: Brace the belly
steps.action: Tighten the belly and press your lower back lightly against the pad.
steps.feel: Belly firm, lower back touching the pad.
steps.visualCheck: Side: no gap between the lower back and the pad.

steps.title: Lift the knees
steps.action: Raise your knees toward your chest until your thighs are about level with your hips; do not swing.
steps.feel: Front of the hips and lower belly working.
steps.visualCheck: Side: thighs about parallel to the floor; body stays still. Front: knees together, not twisting.

steps.title: Tilt the pelvis (small)
steps.action: At the top, curl your hips up slightly by tightening the lower belly, only if your back stays on the pad.
steps.feel: Lower abs squeeze; no pull in the lower back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: pelvis tips up a little, back still touching the pad.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Lower your knees back down under control, without dropping or swinging.
steps.feel: Abs and hips controlling the weight of the legs.
steps.visualCheck: Side: smooth path; legs do not swing forward or back.

steps.title: Stop at the bottom
steps.action: Pause with the legs hanging and the back on the pad before the next rep; do not let the lower back arch away.
steps.breathing: Breathe in, then out as you lift again.
steps.visualCheck: Side: legs hanging, back still on the pad, no swing.

steps.title: Finish
steps.action: After the last rep, lower your feet to the floor or step, then take your forearms off the pads.
steps.visualCheck: Both feet on the floor before you let go.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging
commonMistakes.text: Swinging. Why: momentum replaces muscle and one source says if you need to swing, the load is too high. Fix: bend the knees, lower slowly and stop at the bottom of every rep.

commonMistakes.title: Lower back peeling off the pad or arching
commonMistakes.text: Lower back peeling off the pad or arching. Why: the pelvis tips forward and the lumbar spine takes the load (coaching sources). Fix: press the back into the pad, shorten the range and stop lowering when the back lifts.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the legs
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the legs. Why: loses the lowering work and can jerk the back. Fix: 3 seconds down.

commonMistakes.title: Using the arms and shoulders to pull
commonMistakes.text: Using the arms and shoulders to pull. Why: shrugging or hanging from the shoulders strains them. Fix: forearms rest on the pads, shoulders down.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting too high or too fast
commonMistakes.text: Lifting too high or too fast. Why: no extra benefit above about hip height (one source) and it encourages swinging. Fix: lift to thigh level, then lower.

commonMistakes.title: Going straight-leg too early
commonMistakes.text: Going straight-leg too early. Why: the longer lever is harder and tilts the pelvis. Fix: keep the knees bent until you can do 2 x 12 clean bent-knee reps (est.).

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: can briefly raise blood pressure. Fix: breathe out as you lift.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing reps
commonMistakes.text: Rushing reps. Why: loses control. Fix: 2 s up, 1 s pause, 3 s down.

commonMistakes.title: Doing it daily
commonMistakes.text: Doing it daily. Why: recovery. Fix: 2-3 sessions per week with a rest day between (est.).

commonMistakes.title: Slumping the head forward or twisting
commonMistakes.text: Slumping the head forward or twisting. Why: strains the neck and shifts the load. Fix: head in line, knees together.

safetyNotes: Back position: the hip flexors attach to the spine and pelvis, so a weak trunk lets the lower back arch; keep the back on the pad and stop if it peels off. One coaching source says lower back pain usually means the core has disengaged and the pelvis is tipping forward.
Shoulders and wrists: your weight is on the forearms; stop if you feel pinching in the shoulder.
Grip and balance: if your arms tire or your forearms slip, step down immediately.
Pregnancy and postpartum: advice conflicts and no ACOG leg raise statement was found; ask an obstetrician or pelvic floor physiotherapist, and stop if the belly "cones" or domes.

Osteoporosis: UK consensus guidance advises avoiding postures with a high degree of spinal flexion; the leg raise is not clearly covered, so ask a doctor or physiotherapist; keep the back on the pad, do not curl hard.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure.
Spotter: not needed. Staff can check the station the first time.
Equipment check: pads intact, frame steady, no loose bolts.
Gym etiquette: wipe the pads and handles; do not hog the station between sets; ask staff before filming and do not film other members.

The 150/100 degree hip thresholds, 130 degree knee limit, 3 s minimum rep, sets, reps, rest, tempo and progression steps are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: an ACSM, ACE, NSCA, NHS, Mayo Clinic or Harvard Health captain's chair page or prescription; ExRx muscle lists for the vertical leg raise; EMG data for the captain's chair itself (only a hanging knee-up with straps was found); joint-angle standards for the knee raise; a controlled trial of rep ranges; an ACOG statement on leg raises; an osteoporosis source naming leg raises specifically; condition-specific sources for knee pain, shoulder problems, obesity, PCOS and lower back pain with this exercise.
